text: Both Azure and AWS let default encryption just happen using a key they generate and manage for you. But you can also take the key over yourself. This lesson covers the real tradeoff between those two paths — platform-managed and customer-managed keys — and the compliance reason some organizations require the second one.

A platform-managed key is what's already protecting your Storage Account or S3 bucket the moment you create it, with zero setup. The provider generates the key, stores it, rotates it on its own internal schedule, and manages its entire lifecycle — you never see or touch it. That's exactly why default encryption needs no configuration. The tradeoff: no custom rotation schedule, no detailed per-key usage log, and no way to revoke it yourself.

A customer-managed key, or CMK, flips that. You generate or import the key yourself in Key Vault or KMS, then point your resource at that specific key instead of the provider's default. Now you set the rotation schedule, you can see every encrypt and decrypt operation against it in the audit log, and you decide when to revoke or delete it — real, demonstrable control the provider never had before.

Strip it down to four questions. Setup: platform-managed is automatic, CMK takes real configuration. Control: platform-managed gives none, CMK gives full control over rotation and access. Audit: platform-managed shows nothing specific, CMK logs every use. Compliance: regulated industries routinely require CMKs as documented proof that the customer, not the vendor, controls access to the data.

CMKs carry a real risk platform-managed keys don't: delete or lose that key, and the data it protected becomes permanently, cryptographically unreadable. There's no recovery path, because the entire point is that nobody, not even the cloud provider, can bypass it. Done deliberately, that's called crypto-shredding — an instant, irreversible way to destroy access to everything the key protects.
Keys protect data sitting still. The next lesson shifts to data on the move: TLS and encryption in transit, and how cloud services enforce it by default.
